name: Sa'id ibn Kathir ibn Ufayr
nameAr: سعيد بن كثير بن عُفَير بن مسلم الأنصاري مولاهم المصري

orthography.spelled: Ufayr: with an unpointed ayn and a fa, in the diminutive (عُفَير). He is usually named after his grandfather, Sa'id ibn Ufayr.
orthography.source: Taqrib al-Tahdhib, entry 2382; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari on hadith 71

bornNote: 146 or 147 AH (Shamela narrator record, from the rijal works)

taqrib.ar: صدوق عالم بالأنساب وغيرها، قال الحاكم: يقال إن مصر لم تخرج أجمع للعلوم منه، وقد رد ابن عدي على السعدي في تضعيفه
taqrib.en: Truthful; learned in genealogy and other fields. Al-Hakim: it is said Egypt never produced anyone who combined more of the sciences. Ibn Adi rebutted al-Sa'di's weakening of him.

role: Teacher of al-Bukhari; Egyptian historian and genealogist

verdicts.ar: لم يكن بالثبت، كان يقرأ من كتب الناس، وهو صدوق
verdicts.en: He was not firm; he would read from other people's books; but he is truthful.

verdicts.ar: وهذا الذي قال السعدي لا معنى له، ولم أسمع أحدا ولا بلغني عن أحد من الناس كلام في سعيد بن كثير بن عفير، وهو عند الناس صدوق ثقة
verdicts.en: On al-Sa'di's charge that he held heterodox views and was confused and unreliable: what al-Sa'di said has no basis; I have heard no one, nor has anything reached me from anyone, criticising Sa'id ibn Kathir ibn Ufayr. To people he is truthful and reliable.

verdicts.ar: يقال إن مصر لم تخرج أجمع للعلوم منه
verdicts.en: It is said that Egypt never produced anyone who combined more of the sciences than he did.
Listed him in al-Thiqat (the reliable narrators).

flags.label: Read from written copies
flags.detail: Abu Hatim's reservation is that he read from other people's books rather than from his own hearing-copies, while still calling him truthful. Al-Sa'di (al-Juzajani) called him confused and unreliable; Ibn Adi rejected this outright, and Ibn Hajar's Taqrib records the rejection. In the Sahih, al-Bukhari relied on him for Ibn Wahb's Egyptian material.

bio: An Egyptian scholar, client of the Ansar, remembered as much for his learning in history and genealogy as for hadith; al-Hakim said Egypt produced no one who gathered more of the sciences. He transmitted Ibn Wahb's hadith to al-Bukhari, and al-Bukhari opened the chapter 'whoever God intends good for' with his narration. Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud (in al-Qadar) also used him, but not al-Tirmidhi or Ibn Majah.
